A large study drawing from the UK Biobank database with
over 470,000 participants looked at sunscreen use and skin
cancer. It found that people who used sunscreen
frequently had higher risks of developing skin cancers. The
analysis showed up to a 292% increased risk of invasive
melanoma for sunscreen users, plus higher rates of basal
cell and squamous cell carcinomas.
These links held even after researchers adjusted for
variables like age, skin type, sunburn history, and outdoor
time. As one of the biggest studies of its kind, it provides
extensive data on real-world habits and health outcomes.
The results have sparked discussion because they contrast
with standard advice on sun protection.
Experts have pointed to possible reasons such as how
sunscreen is applied or combined with other behaviors.
The study highlights patterns in sunscreen use and its
association with skin cancer rates in a large population
group. Source: UK Biobank data analysis as covered in
scientific and media reports on the findings.
